At least thats what <@353136597522448385> suggested me in private. I think that could be a decent proposal for Hegota + removing the cap altogether (if we raise to 64kb in glam, it is what I plan on proposing) I need to stress that this analysis was based on a block gas limit of 60M gas. We are planning to raise this in Glamsterdam I think we should re-do this analysis with BAL optimizations in place and assuming higher block limits to be sure that 64kb is safe CC <@703742742135570499> <@968526635735326741> can you give maybe a gas limit target? This still needs to be discussed in ACD, but my take would be to target 100Million gas second including BAL optimizations. This would allow us to go to 300M blocks assuming a 3s execution window (which also depends on ePBS) ok, i see so 300M block's gas needs to be processable in 3s this actually seems to still be the case judging from the results. maybe <@703742742135570499> can comment. ~~It is a 100M block needs to processable in 1s, so that we can do 300M in 3s~~ ye, corrected the typo My understanding is that a 50M block took 1006ms for 64kb, or am I reading that incorrectly? Various things. - Benchmarks were taken without cache (disabled). This means they have no working pre-fetcher nor can do any optimization whatsoever. Also BALs aren't active, so it's even worse. - They are **THE WORST POSSIBLE CASE**. Thus, we should expect this to be extremely rare/impossible. The cost of setting this up is insane. And on top of that you need a whole new setup for every "worst case". - **18,106 EXTCODESIZE operations per block (all different bytecode contracts)**. Don't even understand how this worst case with no cache is taken as "concerning". Anyways, once we migrate bloatnet to Glamsterdam (please let's make this happen ASAP) we can deploy the attack there and measure the results yeah with BAL the worst case is the best case I'm not saying BALs just allow 256kB. But, they should def help no no, I think 64KB is more than enough but you need to consider the cache case with BALs. its the whole point of BAL after all so actually this is covered by the analysis Right, you would have to deploy 18,106 new contracts of that size before running this attack, which would be expensive in practice. However, I still think it would be nice to run this analysis in a closer scenario to glamsterdam (i.e., including BAL optimizations and higher block limits) >but you need to consider the cache case with BALs. its the whole point of BAL after all >so actually this is covered by the analysis What do you mean, <@687974325072035882> ? How is it covered? the whole point of BAL is that since you know access beforehand, you can just cache (as you warm them) async or put them in MMAP or whatever cache the DB of the client has its covered as in, it is the "warm cache" timings I would say the warm case is more representative of accesses to the same bytecode. If you are loading 18k new contracts, even with pre-fetching, I would expect that performance to be lower, no? no, you can max out the read bandwidth. then you need to redeploy In here notice we had all the 18k different bytecodes in cache (or almost all of them) all of them 64kb This is why is that fast (we never hit disk (or almost never)) But TBF, BALs won't reach this lvl of perf. Is impossible to be as fast as cache even if you pre-load stuff in background. Anyways, I agree we should see MUCH better numbers yeah this is upper bound perf but again, the attack would be 18k contracts, you slow down a block and then 18k contracts useless because they are now cached It would be almost 36k contracts right? As we have 2x the gas limit I mean, I'm fine doing this on Bloatnet (I'm not using my node anymore lol) yeah, I think if we can get this analysis out soonish it would nice If <@968526635735326741> thinks is needed to be 100% sure, let's do it. But we need bloatnet on Glamsterdam to begin with no rush ofc :) I def think we are safe here. But idk, in case there are non-belivers in ACD this can be the final deterministic proof ahahahha i also think it is needed btw. metrics driven. always I don't think we need this analysis before discussing it on ACD. But we definitely need it before the fork 😅 no I think we need it because otherwise we waste people's time also you just generate noise btw, I don't think we need to bloat more contracts, to be honest. I would be happy with taking the repricing approach to this and estimating the performance of a single EXTCODESIZE to 64kb contracts with glamsterdam optimizations. This would mean running the same test for varying numbers of EXTCODESIZE. Would this be easier? Also, I wonder if we should run this on more clients besides geth. I just want to make sure we don;t block futher gas limit increases because we mispriced EXTCODESIZE No not you I was talking in general. I'd prefer to go to ACD with data. Otherwise, we are just noisy and get nowhere The "you" was not related to you. That would be rude EXTCODESIZE is already included in my state access repricing. It uses that `test_account_access` test, <@703742742135570499> . I think it targets a specific set of contract from bloatnet, so maybe we could point it to the 64kb contracts you already bloated? We can't deploy them. If you look at the benchmark, it only goes up to 32. That is because bloatnet would need to "fork" and accept the deployment of bigger contracts for all clients. Hence why isn't doable. We can do it for 32 and 100M and estimate 64 Also notice bloating accounts/state here is useless. Only bytecode size matters. So that'sw why I tested with my local node and a modified version of Geth (I can still run it, I have my old modified DB) SO I can run the bench for 100M gas if you want its sublinear so it should not be an issue to just 2x result I see. That makes it more difficult. I think the issue is that from your data, a cold EXTCODESIZE attack block would perform at 50M gas per second and we want to target 100M gas per second. So, we would need to see a 2x gain from BAL pre-fetching for this attack to perform at 100M gas per second Also, from the numbers I am seeing on repricing, geth is not the worst performer for state access, so the worst client is likely performing even worse So, in order to make sure this bump is safe, we would need to estimate the performance of this opcode for all clients and include BAL optimizations. I am also sensitive to the argument that such an attack block is very unlikely due to the deployment cost. I think this is extremely cautious. Again the impact on disabled cache for pre-warming is really big. On top of that, you could only delay 1 block. If you want to delete 2 you'd have to deploy twice the contracts which is insane The network can afford missing a block This just shows that EXTCODESIZE is not an attack vector in the sense regular use will impact the chain perf for 64kb (Notice also all existing contracts will keep being used, so the amount of 64kb ones will take A LONG TIME to get to a meaningful number and have real impact) Right, this argument is the one that convinces me the most so, this is likely safe I'm happy to discuss btw Not saying this is 100% as I say ofc but I would still like to measure the performance of EXTCODESIZE for 64kb on the amsterdam fork at some point before the fork. Once we have a devnet with the EIP included, it would be easier to benchmark, right? CALL and CALLCODE are the current worst performers, so after the bump in state access cost caused by these opcode, the perf of EXTCODESIZE may even be ok I take back what I said, maybe we should attempt to go to ACD with 64kb limit then you can test on a devnet Not sure how can we have such a devnet. We would need all clients to impl this (Though TBH is easy). I can offer taking these numbers for Geth. If you want more than that, then indeed we need devnet with all clients which is much harder (though now that I think it, I should be able to just test with all clients in `dev` mode right? At the end, state size doesn't affect EXTCODESIZE (besides the account read part) Ask claude to make you a kurtosis devnet It works Literally just bump the code size in geth and ask claude. Very good at running kurtosis

excerpts.author: cperezz.eth
excerpts.content:
Various things. 

- Benchmarks were taken without cache (disabled). This means they have no working pre-fetcher nor can do any optimization whatsoever. Also BALs aren't active, so it's even worse.
- They are **THE WORST POSSIBLE CASE**. Thus, we should expect this to be extremely rare/impossible. The cost of setting this up is insane. And on top of that you need a whole new setup for every "worst case".
- **18,106 EXTCODESIZE operations per block (all different bytecode contracts)**. Don't even understand how this worst case with no cache is taken as "concerning".
